Charlie, good to see you.
Thank you, Chief.
In our last meeting, we made an important decision. You’ve been selected to lead your own space mission as the Commander.
My own mission?
That’s right. You’ll choose where you want to go, what you want to investigate, and how you’ll prepare your spacecraft and crew.
That’s a big responsibility.
It is. So, Commander… where do you want to go? Well then, best of luck!!
Hey there, little learner! As you can see, I have just received a huge responsibility. I must succeed no matter what!!
As one of my closest friends, I want you to help me complete the mission. Don’t worry. I am always here to guide you. Now let’s start with the planet selection!
What exactly will we be looking for? Great! Now lets decide what exactly we will be looking for.

That depends on your mission objective. Think carefully.Your objective will determine what location is best, what kind of spacecraft, instruments, rover, power system, and other equipment you’ll need.
It depends on our mission objective. Think carefully. Our objective will determine what location is best, what kind of spacecraft, instruments, rover, power system, and other equipment we’ll need.
Now that our mission is fixed, we will choose the landing site.
You’ll have a limited budget, mass, and power supply. Every choice comes with a trade-off.
Then I’d better choose wisely.
That’s what I want to hear. Your mission begins now, Commander. Make every decision count.
We must remember that we’ll have limited budget, mass, and power supply. Every choice we make, comes with a trade-off.
Now I thing we are good to go. Let’s dive into the mission, mate!

Ascent. Going up from the Moon. The upper cabin takes two explorers back to their friend in orbit.
Docking. Joining two spacecraft gently. Line them up and move slowly, like joining two toy blocks.
Heat shield. A special layer that protects the cabin from very hot air. Point the wide shield forward when coming back to Earth.
Re-entry. Coming back into the air around Earth. Earth’s air slows our cabin. The shield keeps the heat outside.
Parachutes. Big cloth shapes that catch air and slow a falling cabin. They open near Earth. The Moon has no thick air, so we use engines there.
Mineral. A natural solid that can be an ingredient of a rock. One rock can contain several minerals. Matching tools help us find which ones.
Plagioclase. A mineral often found in pale Moon rocks. It can be in other rock types too. Check a second kind of clue before naming the rock.
Elements. Tiny kinds of building pieces that make up rocks and other things. Calcium and aluminium are two kinds. A scanner checks which pieces a rock contains.
Ancient crust rock. A rock rich in pale minerals called plagioclase. Many Moon highland rocks are like this. Light and element clues help us check.
Lava rock. Rock made when hot melted rock cools. We look for matching mineral and element clues before naming it.
Impact-mixed rock. Different broken rock pieces joined together. A big space-rock crash can break and mix Moon rocks. A mixed soil sample alone is not proof.
Element scanner. A tool that checks which tiny building pieces are in a rock. Elements are like ingredients. This tool checks them, not how the crystals are arranged.
Crystal lab. A tool that finds minerals by how their tiny pieces are arranged. First collect a sample. Then the lab checks its crystal pattern.
Layer radar. A tool that listens for radio echoes from under the ground. An echo can show a boundary. It cannot name a rock’s ingredients.
Moonquake sensor. A tool that records tiny shakes in the ground. Put it away from moving wheels. One short reading cannot tell us everything inside the Moon.
Rock sample. A small piece of rock or soil saved for testing. A scoop takes a surface piece. A drill can take deeper material. Keep its place and depth label.
Mission. A job to do in space. Our job: look for clues of ice on the Moon.
Objective. The thing you want to find or do. Like a treasure hunt: your goal is to find ice clues.
Lander. A spacecraft that lands on the ground. It carries our rover safely down to the Moon.
Rover. A robot with wheels that explores the ground. Like a little car that can work on the Moon!
Mass. How much stuff is in something. We count it in kilograms (kg). More parts add more mass. Our rocket can only carry so much.
Budget. How many coins you can spend. You have 1,000 game coins. Save some by choosing smaller parts.
Credits. The pretend coins we use to buy game parts. 100 credits means 100 game coins. It is not a real price.
Power. How fast something uses energy. A busy drill uses energy faster than a small camera.
Peak load. The most power your equipment needs at one time. When the drill starts, it may need a big burst of power.
Energy. The stored supply that helps things work. A full battery holds more energy than an empty one.
Battery. A box that stores energy to run your robot. In a dark crater, the battery keeps the rover moving.
W · Watts. A number that tells us how fast energy is used or made. A 100 W robot uses energy faster than a 50 W robot.
Wh · Watt-hours. A number that tells us how much energy a battery holds. For the same robot, a bigger Wh number means the battery lasts longer.
Reserve. Energy you save for later. We leave 20% in the battery, like saving a snack for the trip home.
Solar array. Panels that turn sunlight into electricity. They need sunlight. In dark shadow, they cannot charge our battery.
Permanent shadow. A place where sunlight never reaches the ground. Some deep Moon craters stay dark and very cold.
Thermal protection. Layers and heaters that help keep the robot at a safe temperature. Like a warm coat and a heater for our rover.
Navigation. Finding the way to a place. Cameras help our rover spot rocks and choose a safe path.
Communication. Sending messages to someone far away. The rover uses a radio to send its discoveries to the lander.
Radar. A tool that sends out radio waves and listens for them to bounce back. It helps the lander tell how close the ground is.
Antenna. A part that sends and catches radio messages. Like ears for the robot’s radio.
Drill depth. How far your tool digs into the ground. A deeper hole takes more time and battery energy.
Reliability. How often something works without trouble. A higher game rating means a better chance of working well.
Geology. Learning about rocks and the ground. Moon rocks can tell us what happened there long ago.
Crater rim. The edge of a big bowl-shaped hole in the ground. A Moon crater’s edge can get light while its deep floor stays dark.
Payload. The things a rocket is carrying to space. Our lander, rover and tools travel inside the rocket.
Adapter. A joining piece that holds two things together. It holds our explorer firmly inside the rocket.
Fairing. The rocket’s protective cover. It protects our explorer from fast-moving air during launch.
Booster. A rocket part that gives a big push at launch. When its fuel is used up, we let it go to carry less mass.
Suit time · EVA. Time astronauts spend outside their spacecraft. Their suits carry a limited supply. They go back inside before it runs low.
Thrust. The push made by a rocket engine. More upward push helps our lander slow down.
Gravity. The pull that brings things toward a moon or planet. Moon gravity pulls our lander down. The engine helps it land softly.
Abort. Stop the landing when it is unsafe. With enough fuel and height, our crew can climb back toward orbit.
Orbit. Moving around a planet while gravity pulls you toward it. Our spacecraft moves sideways fast enough to keep going around Earth.
Rehearsal. A practice run before the real adventure. Try driving and drilling here. Practice samples earn no science points.
Moon dust. Tiny, sharp bits of Moon soil that stick to tools. Digging can put dust on a camera or solar panel. The Moon has no wind like Earth.
Space radiation. Tiny fast particles and energy from space that can hurt people. During a space-weather alert, our crew stays inside a protective shelter.
Care kit. Cleaning tools packed before launch. Our crew can use one cleaning kit at Base. It improves the view, but some sticky dust stays.
Hydrogen. A tiny building piece of many things, including water. Finding it is a clue. It does not always mean there is ice.
Hydroxyl. A small oxygen-and-hydrogen piece that can be attached to a mineral. It is not a whole water molecule. We need more clues before saying there is water.
Evidence. Clues that help us check an answer. Two tools agreeing gives us a stronger clue than guessing.
Confidence. How sure we are about what a clue means. A faint or mixed clue means we should say we are not sure yet.
NSS. A tool that looks for tiny particle clues called neutrons. It can find hydrogen clues. More tools must check whether there is water ice.
NIRVSS. A tool that studies the ground using light our eyes cannot see. The light can give clues about water and minerals.
TRIDENT. A drill that brings little pieces of Moon soil up to the surface. Other tools can study the pieces it digs up.
MSOLO. A tool that checks gases coming from the soil. It helps scientists look for clues of water and other gases.

Ascent. Going up from the Moon. The upper cabin takes two explorers back to their friend in orbit.
Docking. Joining two spacecraft gently. Line them up and move slowly, like joining two toy blocks.
Heat shield. A special layer that protects the cabin from very hot air. Point the wide shield forward when coming back to Earth.
Re-entry. Coming back into the air around Earth. Earth’s air slows our cabin. The shield keeps the heat outside.
Parachutes. Big cloth shapes that catch air and slow a falling cabin. They open near Earth. The Moon has no thick air, so we use engines there.
Mineral. A natural solid that can be an ingredient of a rock. One rock can contain several minerals. Matching tools help us find which ones.
Plagioclase. A mineral often found in pale Moon rocks. It can be in other rock types too. Check a second kind of clue before naming the rock.
Elements. Tiny kinds of building pieces that make up rocks and other things. Calcium and aluminium are two kinds. A scanner checks which pieces a rock contains.
Ancient crust rock. A rock rich in pale minerals called plagioclase. Many Moon highland rocks are like this. Light and element clues help us check.
Lava rock. Rock made when hot melted rock cools. We look for matching mineral and element clues before naming it.
Impact-mixed rock. Different broken rock pieces joined together. A big space-rock crash can break and mix Moon rocks. A mixed soil sample alone is not proof.
Element scanner. A tool that checks which tiny building pieces are in a rock. Elements are like ingredients. This tool checks them, not how the crystals are arranged.
Crystal lab. A tool that finds minerals by how their tiny pieces are arranged. First collect a sample. Then the lab checks its crystal pattern.
Layer radar. A tool that listens for radio echoes from under the ground. An echo can show a boundary. It cannot name a rock’s ingredients.
Moonquake sensor. A tool that records tiny shakes in the ground. Put it away from moving wheels. One short reading cannot tell us everything inside the Moon.
Rock sample. A small piece of rock or soil saved for testing. A scoop takes a surface piece. A drill can take deeper material. Keep its place and depth label.
Mission. A job to do in space. Our job: look for clues of ice on the Moon.
Objective. The thing you want to find or do. Like a treasure hunt: your goal is to find ice clues.
Lander. A spacecraft that lands on the ground. It carries our rover safely down to the Moon.
Rover. A robot with wheels that explores the ground. Like a little car that can work on the Moon!
Mass. How much stuff is in something. We count it in kilograms (kg). More parts add more mass. Our rocket can only carry so much.
Budget. How many coins you can spend. You have 1,000 game coins. Save some by choosing smaller parts.
Credits. The pretend coins we use to buy game parts. 100 credits means 100 game coins. It is not a real price.
Power. How fast something uses energy. A busy drill uses energy faster than a small camera.
Peak load. The most power your equipment needs at one time. When the drill starts, it may need a big burst of power.
Energy. The stored supply that helps things work. A full battery holds more energy than an empty one.
Battery. A box that stores energy to run your robot. In a dark crater, the battery keeps the rover moving.
W · Watts. A number that tells us how fast energy is used or made. A 100 W robot uses energy faster than a 50 W robot.
Wh · Watt-hours. A number that tells us how much energy a battery holds. For the same robot, a bigger Wh number means the battery lasts longer.
Reserve. Energy you save for later. We leave 20% in the battery, like saving a snack for the trip home.
Solar array. Panels that turn sunlight into electricity. They need sunlight. In dark shadow, they cannot charge our battery.
Permanent shadow. A place where sunlight never reaches the ground. Some deep Moon craters stay dark and very cold.
Thermal protection. Layers and heaters that help keep the robot at a safe temperature. Like a warm coat and a heater for our rover.
Navigation. Finding the way to a place. Cameras help our rover spot rocks and choose a safe path.
Communication. Sending messages to someone far away. The rover uses a radio to send its discoveries to the lander.
Radar. A tool that sends out radio waves and listens for them to bounce back. It helps the lander tell how close the ground is.
Antenna. A part that sends and catches radio messages. Like ears for the robot’s radio.
Drill depth. How far your tool digs into the ground. A deeper hole takes more time and battery energy.
Reliability. How often something works without trouble. A higher game rating means a better chance of working well.
Geology. Learning about rocks and the ground. Moon rocks can tell us what happened there long ago.
Crater rim. The edge of a big bowl-shaped hole in the ground. A Moon crater’s edge can get light while its deep floor stays dark.
Payload. The things a rocket is carrying to space. Our lander, rover and tools travel inside the rocket.
Adapter. A joining piece that holds two things together. It holds our explorer firmly inside the rocket.
Fairing. The rocket’s protective cover. It protects our explorer from fast-moving air during launch.
Booster. A rocket part that gives a big push at launch. When its fuel is used up, we let it go to carry less mass.
Suit time · EVA. Time astronauts spend outside their spacecraft. Their suits carry a limited supply. They go back inside before it runs low.
Thrust. The push made by a rocket engine. More upward push helps our lander slow down.
Gravity. The pull that brings things toward a moon or planet. Moon gravity pulls our lander down. The engine helps it land softly.
Abort. Stop the landing when it is unsafe. With enough fuel and height, our crew can climb back toward orbit.
Orbit. Moving around a planet while gravity pulls you toward it. Our spacecraft moves sideways fast enough to keep going around Earth.
Rehearsal. A practice run before the real adventure. Try driving and drilling here. Practice samples earn no science points.
Moon dust. Tiny, sharp bits of Moon soil that stick to tools. Digging can put dust on a camera or solar panel. The Moon has no wind like Earth.
Space radiation. Tiny fast particles and energy from space that can hurt people. During a space-weather alert, our crew stays inside a protective shelter.
Care kit. Cleaning tools packed before launch. Our crew can use one cleaning kit at Base. It improves the view, but some sticky dust stays.
Hydrogen. A tiny building piece of many things, including water. Finding it is a clue. It does not always mean there is ice.
Hydroxyl. A small oxygen-and-hydrogen piece that can be attached to a mineral. It is not a whole water molecule. We need more clues before saying there is water.
Evidence. Clues that help us check an answer. Two tools agreeing gives us a stronger clue than guessing.
Confidence. How sure we are about what a clue means. A faint or mixed clue means we should say we are not sure yet.
NSS. A tool that looks for tiny particle clues called neutrons. It can find hydrogen clues. More tools must check whether there is water ice.
NIRVSS. A tool that studies the ground using light our eyes cannot see. The light can give clues about water and minerals.
TRIDENT. A drill that brings little pieces of Moon soil up to the surface. Other tools can study the pieces it digs up.
MSOLO. A tool that checks gases coming from the soil. It helps scientists look for clues of water and other gases.
